summary_student.text: Small methane and ethylene gas flames were burned aboard the International Space Station while an electric field was applied to them. The team watched how the electric field pushed the flame, changed its soot, and affected flames close to going out. The record says this was not done for space fire safety, but learning how to steer and steady flames could help design future space combustion devices.

summary_professional.text: Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene laminar diffusion flames, on a gas-jet burner and on the CLD Flame coflow burner, were exposed to an electric field from a high-voltage copper mesh electrode above the burner (up to 10 kV) in ACME in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS. Fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, dilution level and field polarity were varied, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves of chemi-ion current, flame response time, flame shape, luminosity, soot distribution, chemiluminescent emission, soot volume fraction and radiant emission (thermopile detectors) were measured.
